screens.title: Introduction to Data Storage Options in Android
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll explore the main ways Android apps save data so information survives app restarts and device reboots. You'll learn what Shared Preferences are best for, when to use internal files versus external files, and why structured data belongs in a database like SQLite — often accessed through Room. I'll show concrete examples, common beginner mistakes, and how privacy and permissions change your choices. For instance, storing a user's dark-mode setting is different from storing a library of recipe images. We'll also briefly discuss network storage and how local caching combines with remote data. By the end of this lesson you will know practical rules of thumb: use Shared Preferences for small key-value settings, internal storage for app-only files, external storage for user-sharable media with caution, and Room for queryable, relational records. As you follow along, think about a simple app you might build and how these options would map to its data types. That reflection will help you pick the right storage option and avoid common pitfalls like serializing complex objects into preferences or putting sensitive data on external storage.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll build four practical competencies that guide how you design app data. First, you will identify Android storage options so you can name them and recognize the appropriate use cases. That matters because selecting the wrong storage leads to fragile, slow, or insecure apps. Second, you'll understand the trade-offs of complexity, performance, and data shape so you can choose a solution that fits your app's needs. For example, choosing a database when only a few settings are required adds unnecessary complexity. Third, you will differentiate between app-specific private storage and shared external storage, learning how permissions and uninstall behavior affect data lifecycle. This helps you protect user privacy and avoid losing data unexpectedly. Fourth, you will apply these choices in simple scenarios and decide the most appropriate storage for several common data types. Each objective combines description, a short example, and a verified competency milestone that signals readiness. By the end of the activities you should be able to map a data type to the right Android storage option and explain why it was the best choice.

screens.title: Why data persistence matters
screens.narratorSegment: Data persistence is the capability of an app to keep information available after it closes or the device restarts. In practice this means remembering user preferences, preserving user-generated content, and keeping application state consistent. A concrete example is a to-do list: when you add tasks, you expect them to remain if the app is closed; that persistence creates a reliable user experience. Another example is game high scores: storing the top score in a lightweight place ensures the user sees progress across sessions. A common misconception is thinking persistence is only for large apps; even tiny apps need to persist a few values like settings or login tokens. Persistence also interacts with privacy and lifecycle: internal files are removed when the app is uninstalled, while external files may remain. When designing persistence, ask: what is the shape and lifetime of my data, who needs access to it, and what queries will I run? This mental checklist helps you avoid poor choices like stuffing large binary data into key-value storage or placing sensitive data on public storage. Consider the user's expectations first, and pick the storage option that preserves the right data, for the right audience, for the right length of time.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Why data persistence matters
Definition

Persistence means data survives beyond a single run of your app. It is how preferences, user files, and records remain available after restarts.

Concrete example
A to-do list that keeps tasks between sessions so users rely on the app to track work.
Common misconception
Only big apps need persistence. In fact, even a small preference or one high score is meaningful to users.
Why it matters
Good persistence improves UX, prevents data loss, and enables offline features.
Quick checklist
  • Who needs the data?
  • How large is it?
  • Will you query or sort it?
  • Is it sensitive or shared?
Example scenario
Game high score: simple integer persisted as a preference is efficient and appropriate; no database needed.
Key Takeaway

Design persistence around data shape and user expectations to avoid future refactors.

screens.title: Shared Preferences — small key-value storage
screens.narratorSegment: Shared Preferences are a lightweight key-value storage suitable for small collections of primitive data: booleans, integers, floats, longs, and strings. Use them for user preferences like a dark-mode flag, a preferred language, or a single high score integer. A concrete example: saving a boolean named "dark_mode" that persists the user's UI preference so the app launches in the correct theme. Shared Preferences are not designed for lists of complex objects or large data like images. A frequent beginner mistake is serializing complex objects into JSON strings and storing them in preferences; this may work for tiny objects but becomes brittle and slow to maintain. Instead, reserve preferences for small, simple state. Shared Preferences are fast and easy to implement, and they remain private to your app if you use the default mode. Remember, if you need to query, sort, or handle relationships between records, a database is a better fit. Lastly, preferences are not a substitute for secure storage: avoid storing sensitive secrets without additional encryption. Shared Preferences — small key-value storage means use for small primitive settings and flags; avoid storing large or complex objects there.. In practical terms, when to store simple settings and primitive values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Shared Preferences
What it is

A simple dictionary of key-value pairs stored persistently. Best for tiny, app-specific settings.

Example
Save a boolean flag that keeps the user in dark mode across app launches.
Common mistake
Serializing complex objects or long lists into preferences instead of using a database or files.
Quick code example
// Pseudo-Kotlin style example
val prefs = context.getSharedPreferences("settings", Context.MODE_PRIVATE)
val editor = prefs.edit()
editor.putBoolean("dark_mode", true)
editor.apply()

val isDark = prefs.getBoolean("dark_mode", false)
Use apply for async save; get with a default value.
When to use
Preferences, small flags, one-off values.
Avoid
Large lists, binary data, or sensitive tokens without encryption.

screens.title: Internal Storage — private app files
screens.narratorSegment: Internal storage provides private file space that only your app can access. Files saved here are ideal for sensitive data, cached images you don't want shared, or configuration files. A key property is lifecycle: internal files are removed automatically if the user uninstalls the app, which prevents orphaned data. A concrete example is saving a downloaded recipe image that you do not want other apps to access. Because internal storage is private, you don't need external permissions, which simplifies implementation. A common misconception is that internal storage is limited to tiny files — while space is constrained compared to external storage, you can store reasonably sized media if needed. However, for very large shared media or files users must access outside the app, external storage is more appropriate. Always consider backup and storage space: internal files count against the device's storage and may be cleared by the system in low-space scenarios if stored in cache directories. Choose internal storage when privacy and automatic cleanup on uninstall are priorities. Internal Storage — private app files means use internal storage for private files that should be cleaned up on uninstall and that don't need to be shared with other apps.. In practical terms, when files belong only to your app and should be removed on uninstall. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use internal storage for private files that should be cleaned up on uninstall and that don't need to be shared with other apps.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Internal Storage
Definition & properties
  • Private to the app; other apps can't access files.
  • Files are deleted when the app is uninstalled.
  • No runtime permission required for private internal files.
Example
Store a recipe cover image that should be accessible only to your app and removed on uninstall.
Best practices
Use for
Sensitive files, app-only caches, small to medium media intended only for the app.
System behavior
Files can be removed from cache directories under low storage pressure.
Avoid
Storing large user-shareable libraries that the user expects to access outside the app.
Key Takeaway

Internal storage gives privacy and automatic cleanup—prefer it for app-owned files that should not be shared.

screens.title: External Storage — public and shared
screens.narratorSegment: External storage refers to shared device storage such as an SD card or a public partition. It is suitable when users expect to access files outside your app, like large media, exported documents, or photos they share. However, external storage is not private and can be modified or deleted by other apps or the user. This means you should never place sensitive personal data there unless it's encrypted. Another important difference is permissions: accessing external storage usually requires requesting runtime permissions, and your app must handle cases where storage becomes unavailable. A concrete example is saving a recipe cover photo to external storage so the user can find and share it in a gallery. A common misconception is assuming external storage is always available; removable SD cards can be absent, so code must handle storage not present. When choosing between internal and external storage, weigh user access needs, privacy, and permission complexity. External Storage — public and shared means use external storage for user-sharable files but treat it as untrusted and permissioned; never store sensitive data there without encryption.. In practical terms, when files should be user-accessible or shared with other apps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › External Storage
What it means

Shared storage space accessible to the user and other apps. Ideal for large media and files meant to be shared or exported.

Example
Save exported recipe PDFs or photos so the user can open them in other apps or transfer them elsewhere.
Considerations
  • Requires runtime permissions in many cases.
  • Files are public and can be modified or deleted by others.
  • May be unavailable if an external card is removed.
When to prefer
User-sharable content and large media.
Risks
Not secure; treat as untrusted storage unless encrypted.
Key Takeaway

Choose external storage when users need to access or share files outside the app, but add permission checks and treat files as untrusted.

screens.title: Files and storage lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing where to store a file follows a simple decision process. First, ask who should access the file. If only your app needs it, internal storage is the default. Second, consider size and user expectations: if the user expects to open or share a file from outside the app, external storage makes sense. Third, evaluate sensitivity: if the data is sensitive, avoid external storage unless you encrypt it. Fourth, think about lifetime: cache files that can be discarded under low storage belong in cache directories, while persistent files belong in files directories. A concrete example is a recipe cover image you download for offline use. If it's only for in-app use and contains no private metadata, store it in internal files. If the user asked to export it to the gallery, move or copy it to external storage and request permission. Common mistakes include assuming external storage is always available and not checking for permission or presence. Follow this checklist and you can implement a robust file strategy that handles permissions, removal on uninstall, and offline behavior gracefully. Files and storage lifecycle means ask: who needs access, how large, how long, and is it sensitive? use internal for private, external for shared, cache for temporary.. In practical terms, how to decide between internal, external, and cached files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Files & Lifecycle
Step 1 — Who needs access?
Private to app → internal. User or other apps → external.
Step 2 — Size & expectation
Large media often belongs on external storage where users can manage it.
Step 3 — Sensitivity
Encrypt before putting sensitive data on external storage, or keep it internal.
Concrete example
A downloaded recipe image: store in internal files for offline in-app display. If the user chooses to export or share, copy it to external storage and handle permissions.
Common pitfall
Failing to check for external storage presence or requesting permissions at runtime can cause crashes or broken behavior. Always guard file operations and provide fallback paths.
Key Takeaway

Follow the access-size-sensitivity-lifetime checklist to pick internal, external, or cache storage.

screens.title: Databases and SQLite
screens.narratorSegment: Databases are the right tool when your app stores structured records that need querying, sorting, or relationships. Android uses SQLite, a lightweight relational database embedded in the device. Use a database when you have many records, like notes, contacts, or journal entries, and when you want efficient queries for filtering or sorting. For example, a notes app that supports searching by date and keyword needs a database rather than preferences or files. Direct SQLite access requires S Q L knowledge and careful query management; novices may write buggy S Q L or forget to close cursors. That's why higher-level libraries help. A common misconception is that databases are overkill for a small number of items; while true for tiny datasets, plan for growth. If you expect lists of records to grow or require complex queries, adopt a database early to avoid costly migrations later. Remember databases store structured text and numeric data well, but large binary blobs like images are often better kept as files with only their paths stored in the database. Databases and SQLite means choose a database for structured records when you need efficient querying, sorting, or relationships between data.. In practical terms, structured, queryable storage for records and relations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Databases & SQLite
Why use a database
  • Efficient queries and filters for many records.
  • Structured schema and relationships between entities.
  • Better growth characteristics than ad-hoc files or preferences.
Practical example
A journal app where entries are searchable by date and keyword should use a database for speed and flexibility.
Common misconception
Databases are only for massive apps. In reality, adopting a database early avoids brittle workarounds when records grow.
Note on binary data
Store large images as files and keep their file paths in the database instead of placing binary blobs inside rows.
Key Takeaway

When you need queries, sorts, or relationships, a database is the robust solution.

screens.title: Room Persistence Library
screens.narratorSegment: Room is an Android Jetpack library that wraps SQLite and gives you a type-safe, annotated Kotlin layer for working with databases. It reduces boilerplate, enforces compile-time checks for S Q L queries, and integrates with other Jetpack components like LiveData and ViewModel. A concrete example: instead of writing raw S Q L to query recent notes, you define a data class as an entity, annotate it, and write a DAO method that returns a list of entities. Room validates queries at compile time, avoiding runtime surprises from malformed S Q L. A common misconception is that Room removes the need to understand S Q L; while Room simplifies many tasks, you still need to know how to structure queries and relationships. The main benefits are safety, maintainability, and easier migrations. Use Room when your app needs structured records and you want to align with Android best practices. Storing entity objects and letting Room handle persistence leads to cleaner, less error-prone code than manual cursor management. screens.title: Local vs Network storage
screens.narratorSegment: Network storage refers to data kept on remote servers or cloud services, used when data must be shared across devices, updated frequently, or is too large for local storage. In practice a robust app blends network and local storage: fetch authoritative data from the network and cache it locally for offline use and performance. For example, a recipe app might fetch a recipe catalog from a server but cache recently viewed recipes in a local database so users can open them without connectivity. When caching decide what to store locally, how to invalidate stale data, and how to handle conflicts when offline edits need syncing. screens.title: Common pitfalls and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Developers commonly make a few repeating mistakes when choosing storage. One is serializing complex objects into Shared Preferences. While stringifying an object can work for simple cases, it quickly becomes fragile as the object evolves. A safer pattern is to use a database or files for complex data. Another frequent error is storing sensitive user information on external storage where other apps or users can read it. If you must store sensitive data outside your private storage, apply encryption and treat the storage as untrusted. A third mistake is failing to handle external storage absence or missing permissions; always check for permission and storage availability and provide fallbacks. Finally, putting large binary data in a database row can bloat queries; instead store files and record paths in the database. Practical best practices: choose the simplest storage that meets your needs, plan for schema changes if using a database, and document where each type of data is stored. These habits reduce bugs and future maintenance. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll explore the main ways Android apps save data so information survives app restarts and device reboots. You'll learn what Shared Preferences are best for, when to use internal files versus external files, and why structured data belongs in a database like SQLite — often accessed through Room. I'll show concrete examples, common beginner mistakes, and how privacy and permissions change your choices. For instance, storing a user's dark-mode setting is different from storing a library of recipe images. We'll also briefly discuss network storage and how local caching combines with remote data. By the end of this lesson you will know practical rules of thumb: use Shared Preferences for small key-value settings, internal storage for app-only files, external storage for user-sharable media with caution, and Room for queryable, relational records. As you follow along, think about a simple app you might build and how these options would map to its data types. That reflection will help you pick the right storage option and avoid common pitfalls like serializing complex objects into preferences or putting sensitive data on external storage.

In this chapter you'll build four practical competencies that guide how you design app data. First, you will identify Android storage options so you can name them and recognize the appropriate use cases. That matters because selecting the wrong storage leads to fragile, slow, or insecure apps. Second, you'll understand the trade-offs of complexity, performance, and data shape so you can choose a solution that fits your app's needs. For example, choosing a database when only a few settings are required adds unnecessary complexity. Third, you will differentiate between app-specific private storage and shared external storage, learning how permissions and uninstall behavior affect data lifecycle. This helps you protect user privacy and avoid losing data unexpectedly. Fourth, you will apply these choices in simple scenarios and decide the most appropriate storage for several common data types. Each objective combines description, a short example, and a verified competency milestone that signals readiness. By the end of the activities you should be able to map a data type to the right Android storage option and explain why it was the best choice.

This screen focuses on how you'll demonstrate the objectives by doing short, practical checks. You'll practice naming which storage to use for five example data items, explain the reasoning in two sentences, and identify potential privacy risks. For instance, when an image must be private and available offline, internal storage is the best fit; when the same image must be user-accessible across apps, external storage is a candidate but requires permission. You'll also practice detecting misuse, such as serializing complex objects into Shared Preferences, which leads to brittle code and maintenance headaches. Finally, you will be guided to a small milestone: map five data types from a sample app to a storage choice and write the short justification. These small activities build the habit of matching data shape, size, and access pattern to the correct Android storage mechanism. Completing them confirms you can explain a choice and reason about alternatives.

Data persistence is the capability of an app to keep information available after it closes or the device restarts. In practice this means remembering user preferences, preserving user-generated content, and keeping application state consistent. A concrete example is a to-do list: when you add tasks, you expect them to remain if the app is closed; that persistence creates a reliable user experience. Another example is game high scores: storing the top score in a lightweight place ensures the user sees progress across sessions. A common misconception is thinking persistence is only for large apps; even tiny apps need to persist a few values like settings or login tokens. Persistence also interacts with privacy and lifecycle: internal files are removed when the app is uninstalled, while external files may remain. When designing persistence, ask: what is the shape and lifetime of my data, who needs access to it, and what queries will I run? This mental checklist helps you avoid poor choices like stuffing large binary data into key-value storage or placing sensitive data on public storage. Consider the user's expectations first, and pick the storage option that preserves the right data, for the right audience, for the right length of time.

Shared Preferences are a lightweight key-value storage suitable for small collections of primitive data: booleans, integers, floats, longs, and strings. Use them for user preferences like a dark-mode flag, a preferred language, or a single high score integer. A concrete example: saving a boolean named "dark_mode" that persists the user's UI preference so the app launches in the correct theme. Shared Preferences are not designed for lists of complex objects or large data like images. A frequent beginner mistake is serializing complex objects into JSON strings and storing them in preferences; this may work for tiny objects but becomes brittle and slow to maintain. Instead, reserve preferences for small, simple state. Shared Preferences are fast and easy to implement, and they remain private to your app if you use the default mode. Remember, if you need to query, sort, or handle relationships between records, a database is a better fit. Lastly, preferences are not a substitute for secure storage: avoid storing sensitive secrets without additional encryption. Shared Preferences — small key-value storage means use for small primitive settings and flags; avoid storing large or complex objects there.. In practical terms, when to store simple settings and primitive values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Internal storage provides private file space that only your app can access. Files saved here are ideal for sensitive data, cached images you don't want shared, or configuration files. A key property is lifecycle: internal files are removed automatically if the user uninstalls the app, which prevents orphaned data. A concrete example is saving a downloaded recipe image that you do not want other apps to access. Because internal storage is private, you don't need external permissions, which simplifies implementation. A common misconception is that internal storage is limited to tiny files — while space is constrained compared to external storage, you can store reasonably sized media if needed. However, for very large shared media or files users must access outside the app, external storage is more appropriate. Always consider backup and storage space: internal files count against the device's storage and may be cleared by the system in low-space scenarios if stored in cache directories. Choose internal storage when privacy and automatic cleanup on uninstall are priorities. Internal Storage — private app files means use internal storage for private files that should be cleaned up on uninstall and that don't need to be shared with other apps.. In practical terms, when files belong only to your app and should be removed on uninstall. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

External storage refers to shared device storage such as an SD card or a public partition. It is suitable when users expect to access files outside your app, like large media, exported documents, or photos they share. However, external storage is not private and can be modified or deleted by other apps or the user. This means you should never place sensitive personal data there unless it's encrypted. Another important difference is permissions: accessing external storage usually requires requesting runtime permissions, and your app must handle cases where storage becomes unavailable. A concrete example is saving a recipe cover photo to external storage so the user can find and share it in a gallery. A common misconception is assuming external storage is always available; removable SD cards can be absent, so code must handle storage not present. When choosing between internal and external storage, weigh user access needs, privacy, and permission complexity. Choosing where to store a file follows a simple decision process. First, ask who should access the file. If only your app needs it, internal storage is the default. Second, consider size and user expectations: if the user expects to open or share a file from outside the app, external storage makes sense. Third, evaluate sensitivity: if the data is sensitive, avoid external storage unless you encrypt it. Fourth, think about lifetime: cache files that can be discarded under low storage belong in cache directories, while persistent files belong in files directories. A concrete example is a recipe cover image you download for offline use. If it's only for in-app use and contains no private metadata, store it in internal files. If the user asked to export it to the gallery, move or copy it to external storage and request permission. Databases are the right tool when your app stores structured records that need querying, sorting, or relationships. Android uses SQLite, a lightweight relational database embedded in the device. For each data item decide the storage and justify it. 1) Dark-mode preference: store as a boolean in Shared Preferences because it is a small primitive setting that must persist across launches. 2) List of user-created recipes: use Room because recipes have structured fields — title, ingredients, instructions — and you will want to search and sort them. 3) Large cover photo downloaded for offline use but private to the app: store the image in internal storage, keeping the path in the database if needed. 4) A temporary debug log: write to internal cache or files so it is private and removed on uninstall or by the system. 5) User shopping list where items can be added and removed: use Room for structured operations or a small local file if the list is tiny and performance isn't a concern. For each choice, also state a risk: for external files mention permissions and lack of privacy; for preferences mention not storing complex objects. This mapping practice helps you make defensible decisions under real constraints.

Developers commonly make a few repeating mistakes when choosing storage. One is serializing complex objects into Shared Preferences. While stringifying an object can work for simple cases, it quickly becomes fragile as the object evolves. A safer pattern is to use a database or files for complex data. Another frequent error is storing sensitive user information on external storage where other apps or users can read it. If you must store sensitive data outside your private storage, apply encryption and treat the storage as untrusted. A third mistake is failing to handle external storage absence or missing permissions; always check for permission and storage availability and provide fallbacks. Finally, putting large binary data in a database row can bloat queries; instead store files and record paths in the database. Practical best practices: choose the simplest storage that meets your needs, plan for schema changes if using a database, and document where each type of data is stored. These habits reduce bugs and future maintenance. Let's summarize the most important terms from this chapter. Data persistence means storing information that survives app restarts and device reboots. Shared Preferences are a simple key-value store for small primitives like flags and simple settings. Internal storage is private to your app and files there are removed on uninstall. Each concept maps to practical choices: small settings stay in preferences, private app files in internal storage, and structured records in databases. Knowing these definitions helps you pick a storage strategy quickly and explain your design choices to others. Keep these concise definitions in mind as mental shorthand: size and structure guide your storage, and privacy and access guide internal versus external choices. Remember, these are rules of thumb, not iron laws — use them as a starting point and adapt when edge cases appear.

Finish with the remaining essential terms. External Storage is public and shared, suitable for user-accessible media but not for sensitive data unless encrypted. SQLite is the embedded relational engine for structured data on Android. The Room Persistence Library sits on top of SQLite to provide type-safe Kotlin APIs, compile-time S Q L checks, and easier integration with app architecture. Finally, network storage holds authoritative or shared datasets on servers; pair it with local caching for offline support and improved performance. These terms form the decision vocabulary you'll use when designing app storage. Keep the trade-offs in mind: accessibility, privacy, query capability, and lifecycle behavior determine the right choice. When in doubt, prefer the simplest, safest option that meets user expectations and plan migration paths for growth.
